body:
1.1 What are the most common types of private equity transactions in your jurisdiction? What is the current state of the market for these transactions?

In 2025, add-on acquisitions and buyouts were the most common types of private equity (PE) transactions in Australia. Of the 147 reported PE transactions, totalling an aggregate value of A$13.6 billion, approximately 79 were add-on acquisitions and approximately 24 were buyouts.1,2

For the last 11 years, these two types of transactions have been the most prevalent in Australia, consistently comprising approximately 70% of PE deals. Although buyouts historically represented the majority of these deals, add-ons have gradually become the most common type in terms of percentage of total deals in Australia.3

As of June 2025, Australian PE funds managed A$51.5 billion in assets under management (AUM) (with about one-quarter being dry powder), a 13% increase since June 2023.4

The Australian Investment Council (AIC) 2026 Yearbook stated that, while the technology sector has emerged as the primary investment target (accounting for approximately one-third of PE transactions in 2025), other industries such as business services, consumer discretionary, healthcare, and finance and insurance continue to attract PE interest.5

The largest purely PE-backed deals in Australia over the last two years have been in the telecoms and media industry (DAZN’s acquisition of Foxtel) as well as the finance and insurance industry (One Investment Management and CC Capital’s acquisition of Insignia Financial and The Ardonagh Group’s acquisition of PSC Insurance Group).6 The acquisitions of Insignia Financial and PSC Insurance Group were take-private transactions by schemes of arrangement, indicating strong momentum in the public-to-private transaction space.

1.2 What are the most significant factors currently encouraging or inhibiting private equity transactions in your jurisdiction?

Higher interest rates correlate with reduced private capital fundraising, as low-risk investments such as bonds become increasingly attractive. With rising inflation figures and the threat of further interest rate increases, asset valuations and exit opportunities have required reassessment by PE investors. Despite this, the Australian fundraising scene has proven resilient, with 6% growth from 2024 to 2025, differentiating itself from the Asia Pacific region (excluding Australia), which fell 45% in that same period. Moreover, research from Cambridge Associates showed that, as of September 2025, the Australian PE index outperformed global peers over five years (19.5% net internal rate of return (IRR)) and has demonstrated comparable results with global peers at the three- and 10-year sample.

Regulatory scrutiny has also increased, particularly from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and the Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) (see questions 11.1 and 11.2 below for further details).

1.3 Are you seeing any types of investors other than traditional private equity firms executing private equity-style transactions in your jurisdiction? If so, please explain which investors, and briefly identify any significant points of difference between the deal terms offered, or approach taken, by this type of investor and that of traditional private equity firms.

Superannuation (pension) funds, sovereign wealth funds and large family office investors continue to seek more co-investment opportunities with PE funds. This reduces the need for “club deals” for PE funds on larger acquisitions and gives small- and mid-cap funds exposure to larger deals than would normally be available to them.

2.1 What are the most common acquisition structures adopted for private equity transactions in your jurisdiction?

The most common acquisition structure for a leveraged deal involves a three-level “stack” of Australian-incorporated private holding companies, with PE investors and management taking equity in the top entity (HoldCo or TopCo), bank debt coming in at the second level (FinCo or MidCo) and the acquisition being made by this entity’s subsidiary (BidCo). The acquisition is typically made by way of share acquisition rather than business and asset acquisition. There is no concept of a merger in Australian law.

2.2 What are the main drivers for these acquisition structures?

The three-tiered “stack” structure provides structural subordination for financiers, with funding entering at FinCo (middle) level, positioned below the equity interests of the PE fund and management team (at HoldCo/TopCo level).

From a tax perspective, the structure permits deductibility of interest on acquisition debt repayments (subject to integrity regimes) and typically reduces the risk of unintended consequences when acquiring an existing tax consolidated group.

2.3 How is the equity commonly structured in private equity transactions in your jurisdiction (including institutional, management and carried interests)?

generally contains compulsory acquisition requirements and transfer restrictions; and

may involve a ratchet on returns on exit.

PE investors’ general partners (GPs) tend to receive 20% carry after repayment of debts and after meeting an agreed IRR per annum (usually around 8%).

2.4 If a private equity investor is taking a minority position, are there different structuring considerations?

Generally, there are no material differences in structuring a minority position, except that a minority PE investor:

may protect their downside risk by seeking preference rights on a liquidation, including subscribing for convertible preference shares; and

will structure the governance arrangements to impose voting, veto and other control rights in respect of certain matters, given that it will not otherwise have any control at the board or shareholder level.

2.5 In relation to management equity, what is the typical range of equity allocated to the management, and what are the typical vesting and compulsory acquisition provisions?

Management is typically allocated 5–15% of HoldCo’s equity.

Compulsory acquisition provisions are often triggered by becoming a “leaver”, material breach of the shareholders’ agreement or insolvency. The Australian Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) (Corporations Act) regulates a company’s acquisition of its own shares, with the process being much more burdensome than cancelling options. Vesting is more commonly applied to options rather than equity; however, “vesting” can be achieved in respect of equity allocated to the management by contractually agreeing different values to the equity, upon compulsory acquisition or an exit, depending on whether or not the equity has “vested”.

2.6 For what reasons is a management equity holder usually treated as a good leaver or a bad leaver in your jurisdiction?

Australian leaver provisions are generally more bespoke than in other jurisdictions.

A good leaver is generally a manager who “leaves” employment because of death, permanent disability or incapacity, redundancy, or is otherwise deemed a good leaver through board discretion. Typically, their shares are able to be compulsorily acquired for the higher of cost or fair market value (FMV).

A bad leaver is generally a manager who “leaves” employment but is not a good leaver. Typically, their shares are compulsorily acquired for the lower of cost and FMV (sometimes with a discount to reflect the cost of effecting the compulsory acquisition (e.g. the acquisition price may be 90% of the lower of cost and FMV)).

Intermediate leaver provisions are uncommon.

3.1 What are the typical governance arrangements for private equity portfolio companies? Are such arrangements required to be made publicly available in your jurisdiction?

PE portfolio companies are customarily private companies governed by a constitution (addressing generic corporate matters) and a shareholders’ agreement between the PE investor, managers, other share or right holders, and the company (addressing bespoke governance, exit and operational matters). If there is inconsistency between the governance documents, the terms of the shareholders’ agreement typically prevail.

Private companies’ governance documents are not required to be publicly available.

3.2 Do private equity investors and/or their director nominees typically enjoy veto rights over major corporate actions (such as acquisitions and disposals, business plans, related party transactions, etc.)? If a private equity investor takes a minority position, what veto rights would they typically enjoy?

Nominee directors of controlling PE investors generally control the board’s majority vote and therefore do not require veto rights.

Minority PE investors normally have limited veto rights, generally restricted to key constitutional issues, along with material changes and transactions.

3.3 Are there any limitations on the effectiveness of veto arrangements: (i) at the shareholder level; and (ii) at the director nominee level? If so, how are these typically addressed?

Certain corporate actions (e.g. adopting a constitution) can only be effected under the Corporations Act by a special resolution of shareholders (at least 75% of voting shares). However, a shareholders’ agreement may permit a shareholder with less than 25% of voting shares to veto such matters.

Even if a nominee director is entitled to act in the best interest of their appointor (the PE investor), general fiduciary and statutory directors’ duties still apply, including to: act with care and diligence; act in good faith; act for a proper purpose; not misuse their position; prevent insolvent trading; avoid conflicts; and not fetter their discretion.

3.4 Are there any duties owed by a private equity investor to minority shareholders such as management shareholders (or vice versa)? If so, how are these typically addressed?

PE investors do not owe specific duties to minority or management shareholders (or vice versa); however, their nominee directors are subject to a duty to act in the best interests of the portfolio company as a whole (i.e. including all of its shareholders).

In addition, minority shareholders:

may have constitutional and/or shareholders’ agreement protections; and

have statutory and common law protections (e.g. prohibition on minority shareholder oppression).

3.5 Are there any limitations or restrictions on the contents or enforceability of shareholder agreements (including (i) governing law and jurisdiction, and (ii) non-compete and non-solicit provisions)?

Generally, there are no limitations or restrictions on shareholders’ agreements, except:

general prohibitions on enforcing terms that are, for example, contrary to public policy, oppress the minority or are construed as an unenforceable penalty; and

restraints must protect a legitimate business interest and be reasonable (including the duration of the restraint period and the breadth of the geographical restriction, which are often cascaded to strengthen enforceability). Recent legislative amendments have resulted in the ACCC reviewing restraint of trade clauses with additional scrutiny and requiring parties to justify the addition of such clauses when lodging a notification for antitrust approval, as described in question 4.1 below.

3.6 Are there any legal restrictions or other requirements that a private equity investor should be aware of in appointing its nominees to boards of portfolio companies? What are the key potential risks and liabilities for (i) directors nominated by private equity investors to portfolio company boards, and (ii) private equity investors that nominate directors to boards of portfolio companies?

Nominee directors should be aware of their directors’ duties (see question 3.3 above).

p: 1.1 What are the most common types of private equity transactions in your jurisdiction? What is the current state of the market for these transactions?
2025년 기준, 호주에서 가장 흔한 유형의 PE 거래는 애드온 인수(add-on acquisitions)와 바이아웃이었다. 총 147건의 보고된 PE 거래 중 총 거래액은 136억 호주 달러에 달했으며, 약 79건이 애드온 인수, 약 24건이 바이아웃이었다.1,2
지난 11년 동안 이 두 가지 거래 유형은 호주에서 가장 주를 이루었으며, 지속적으로 PE 딜의 약 70%를 차지해 왔다. 역사적으로는 바이아웃이 이러한 딜의 대다수를 차지했으나, 호주 전체 딜 비중 측면에서는 애드온 인수가 점차 가장 흔한 유형이 되었다.3
2025년 6월 기준, 호주 PE 운용사들은 515억 호주 달러 규모의 운용자산(AUM)을 관리하고 있으며(약 4분의 1이 드라이 파우더임), 이는 2023년 6월 이후 13% 증가한 수치이다.4
Australian Investment Council (AIC) 2026 Yearbook에 따르면, 기술 부문이 주요 투자처로 부상한 반면(2025년 PE 거래의 약 3분의 1을 차지), 비즈니스 서비스, 경기소비재, 헬스케어, 금융 및 보험 등의 다른 산업들도 계속해서 PE의 관심을 끌고 있다.5

지난 2년간 호주에서 진행된 순수 PE 백업 딜 중 가장 큰 규모는 텔레콤 및 미디어 산업(DAZN의 Foxtel 인수)과 금융 및 보험 산업(One Investment Management와 CC Capital의 Insignia Financial 인수 및 The Ardonagh Group의 PSC Insurance Group 인수)에서 이루어졌다.6 Insignia Financial과 PSC Insurance Group의 인수는 주식배정계획(schemes of arrangement)을 통한 상장폐지(public-to-private) 거래였으며, 이는 퍼블릭 투 프라이빗 거래 영역에서의 강한 모멘텀을 보여준다.
1.2 What are the most significant factors currently encouraging or inhibiting private equity transactions in your jurisdiction?

금리 상승은 채권과 같은 저위험 투자의 매력이 높아짐에 따라 사모 자본 펀드레이징 감소와 상관관계가 있다. 인플레이션 수치 상승과 추가 금리 인상 위협 속에서, 자산 가치평가와 엑시트 기회는 PE 투자자들의 재평가를 필요로 했다. 그럼에도 불구하고, 호주의 펀드레이징 시장은 2024년부터 2025년까지 6%의 성장을 기록하며 회복력을 입증했고, 같은 기간 45% 하락한 아시아 태평양 지역(호주 제외)과 차별화되었다. 더욱이 Cambridge Associates의 연구에 따르면, 2025년 9월 기준 호주 PE 지수는 5년 동안 글로벌 동종 그룹을 상회하는 성과를 냈으며(19.5%의 순내부수익률(IRR)), 3년 및 10년 표본에서도 글로벌 동종 그룹과 필적하는 결과를 보여주었다.
규제 심사 또한 강화되었으며, 특히 Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC)과 Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB)로부터의 심사가 두드러진다(자세한 내용은 아래 11.1 및 11.2 문항 참조).

1.3 Are you seeing any types of investors other than traditional private equity firms executing private equity-style transactions in your jurisdiction? If so, please explain which investors, and briefly identify any significant points of difference between the deal terms offered, or approach taken, by this type of investor and that of traditional private equity firms.
연기금(superannuation funds), 국부펀드, 대형 패밀리 오피스 투자자들은 PE 펀드와의 공동투자(co-investment) 기회를 계속해서 모색하고 있다. 이는 PE 펀드가 대규모 인수를 진행할 때 "클럽 딜(club deals)"의 필요성을 줄여주고, 소형 및 중형 펀드가 평소 접근하기 어려운 더 큰 딜에 노출될 수 있도록 해준다.
2.1 What are the most common acquisition structures adopted for private equity transactions in your jurisdiction?

레버리지 딜에 채택되는 가장 흔한 인수 구조는 호주에 설립된 3단계 사모 지주회사 "스택(stack)" 구조로, PE 투자자와 경영진이 최상단 법인(HoldCo 또는 TopCo)에 지분을 보유하고, 2단계에 은행 부채가 들어오며(FinCo 또는 MidCo), 이 법인의 자회사(BidCo)가 인수를 실행하는 방식이다. 인수는 일반적으로 영업 및 자산 양수도가 아닌 주식 인수의 방식으로 이루어진다. 호주 법에는 합병(merger)이라는 개념이 없다.
2.2 What are the main drivers for these acquisition structures?
3단계 "스택" 구조는 PE 펀드 및 경영진의 지분(HoldCo/TopCo 수준) 아래에 위치한 FinCo(중간) 수준으로 자금이 유입됨으로써, 자금 제공자들에게 구조적 후순위성(structural subordination)을 제공한다.
세무 관점에서, 이 구조는 인수 부채 상환에 대한 이자 공제를 허용하며(무결성 규제 적용 대상), 기존의 세무 통합 그룹을 인수할 때 의도하지 않은 결과가 발생할 위험을 대개 줄여준다.
2.3 How is the equity commonly structured in private equity transactions in your jurisdiction (including institutional, management and carried interests)?
일반적으로 강제 매수 요건과 이전 제한을 포함하며;
엑시트 시 수익에 대한 래칫(ratchet)을 수반할 수 있다.
PE 투자자의 제너럴 파트너(GP)들은 부채 상환 후 그리고 연간 합의된 IRR(통상 약 8%)을 달성한 후에 20%의 캐리(carry)를 받는 경향이 있다.
2.4 If a private equity investor is taking a minority position, are there different structuring considerations?
일반적으로 소수지분 투자를 구조화하는 데 있어 중요한 차이점은 없으나, 소수지분 PE 투자자는 다음의 특징을 갖는다.
전환우선주 인수를 포함하여 청산 시 우선권을 추구함으로써 하방 위험을 방어할 수 있으며;
이사회나 주주 수준에서 달리 통제권을 갖지 못하므로, 특정 사안에 대해 투표권, 거부권 및 기타 지배권 권리를 부과하도록 지배구조를 설계한다.
2.5 In relation to management equity, what is the typical range of equity allocated to the management, and what are the typical vesting and compulsory acquisition provisions?
경영진에게는 대개 HoldCo 지분의 5~15%가 배정된다.

강제 매수 조항은 주로 "리버(leaver)"가 되거나, 주주간 계약을 중대하게 위반하거나, 파산할 때 발동된다. 호주 Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) (Corporations Act)은 회사의 자기주식 취득을 규제하며, 그 절차는 스톡옵션을 취소하는 것보다 훨씬 더 까다롭다. 베스팅(vesting)은 지분보다는 옵션에 더 흔하게 적용된다. 그러나 경영진에게 배정된 지분의 경우, 지분이 "베스팅"되었는지 여부에 따라 강제 매수 또는 엑시트 시 지분에 서로 다른 가치를 부여하기로 계약상 합의함으로써 지분에 대해서도 "베스팅"을 달성할 수 있다.
2.6 For what reasons is a management equity holder usually treated as a good leaver or a bad leaver in your jurisdiction?
호주의 리버 조항은 일반적으로 다른 관할권보다 더 맞춤형으로 구성되어 있다.
굿 리버는 대개 사망, 영구적 장애 또는 무능력, 구조조정으로 인해 고용을 "떠나"거나 이사회의 재량에 따라 굿 리버로 간주되는 경영진이다. 전형적으로 이들의 주식은 취득 원가와 공정시장가치(FMV) 중 높은 금액으로 강제 매수될 수 있다.
배드 리버는 일반적으로 고용을 "떠나"지만 굿 리버가 아닌 경영진이다. 대개 이들의 주식은 취득 원가와 FMV 중 낮은 금액으로 강제 매수된다(강제 매수 집행 비용을 반영하기 위해 때로는 할인율이 적용됨, 예: 인수가격이 취득 원가와 FMV 중 낮은 금액의 90%일 수 있음).
중간 리버(intermediate leaver) 조항은 흔하지 않다.
3.1 What are the typical governance arrangements for private equity portfolio companies? Are such arrangements required to be made publicly available in your jurisdiction?
PE 포트폴리오 회사는 관례적으로 정관(일반적인 기업 사안을 다룸)과 PE 투자자, 경영진, 기타 주주 또는 권리 보유자, 그리고 회사 간의 주주간 계약(맞춤형 지배구조, 엑시트 및 운영 사안을 다룸)에 의해 규율되는 비상장 회사이다. 지배구조 문서 간에 상충이 있는 경우, 주주간 계약의 조건이 우선 적용되는 것이 일반적이다.
비상장 회사의 지배구조 문서는 공개할 의무가 없다.

3.2 Do private equity investors and/or their director nominees typically enjoy veto rights over major corporate actions (such as acquisitions and disposals, business plans, related party transactions, etc.)? If a private equity investor takes a minority position, what veto rights would they typically enjoy?
지배주주인 PE 투자자의 지명 이사들은 일반적으로 이사회 다수결 투표권을 통제하므로 거부권이 필요하지 않다.
소수지분 PE 투자자는 일반적으로 제한된 거부권을 가지며, 이는 대개 핵심 정관 사안과 중대한 변경 및 거래로 한정된다.
3.3 Are there any limitations on the effectiveness of veto arrangements: (i) at the shareholder level; and (ii) at the director nominee level? If so, how are these typically addressed?
